title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Búcar killed and Tizón won; the victory and the spoils (tiradas 118–119, lines 2403–2473)
part: Tiradas 118–119 · Búcar killed and Tizón won; the victory and the spoils (lines 2403–2473)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 280–284, lines 2403–2473 (tiradas 118–119). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
Sácanlos de las tiendas, cáenlos en alcaz;
tanto braço con loriga veriedes caer a part,
tantas cabeças con yelmos que por el campo ca[d]en,
cavallos sin dueños salir a todas partes.
sentences.l:
They-bring-them-out of the tents, they-fall-on-them in pursuit;
so-many-an arm with hauberk you-would-have-seen fall aside,
so-many heads with helmets that through the field fall,
horses without masters go-out to all parts.
sentences.i: They drive them out of the tents and fall on them in pursuit. You would have seen so many a mailed arm fall away, so many helmeted heads tumbling across the field, and riderless horses running off on every side.
sentences.n: Tirada 118 (assonance á) — the Christians pursue the enemy; the Çid overtakes and kills Búcar; he wins the sword Tizón (Pidal: Los cristianos persiguen al enemigo.—El Cid alcanza y mata a Búcar.—Gana la espada Tizón). The line-ends run alcaz, part, ca[d]en, partes, segudar: stressed á, with some lines in á-e (caden, partes, and cade at v. 2415), as in the poem's other á tiradas. Sácanlos de las tiendas takes up the last line of tirada 117 (de las tiendas los sacan): the new tirada opens by repeating the action. cáenlos en alcaz: caer en alcaz, 'to fall to the pursuit' (cade en alcança, v. 2399), here with los, the Moors: 'they fall on them in pursuit'; alcaz, 'pursuit, chase'. tanto braço, singular, 'so many an arm'; loriga, 'hauberk, coat of mail', whose sleeve covered the arm. veriedes, 'you would have seen', the singer to his hearers, governing the infinitives caer and salir. a part, 'aside, apart', lopped away. ca[d]en = caen, the d Pidal's (in italics). dueños, 'masters, owners'. Pidal's note to v. 2404: Esta descripción está imitada de las Chansons de geste francesas, p. 39-40 — 'this description is imitated from the French chansons de geste' (pages of his introduction).

sentences.t: Siete migeros complidos duró el segudar.
sentences.l: Seven miles full lasted the pursuing.
sentences.i: For seven full miles the pursuit went on.
sentences.n: migeros, 'miles'; complidos = cumplidos, 'complete, full'. el segudar, the infinitive used as a noun, 'the pursuing' (segudar, 'to pursue'). Pidal's note: 'Siete millas completas duró la persecución de los fugitivos' — 'the pursuit of the fugitives lasted seven full miles'.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid al rey Búcar ca[d]iól en alcaz:
“Acá torna, Búcar! venist dalent mar.
Ve[e]rte as con el Çid, el de la barba grant,
saludar nos hemos amos, e tajaremos amizta[t].”
sentences.l:
My Çid to-the king Búcar fell-on-him in pursuit:
“Hither turn, Búcar! you-came from-beyond sea.
You-will-see-yourself with the Çid, he of the beard great,
greet ourselves we-shall both, and we-shall-cut friendship.”
sentences.i: My Çid went after King Búcar in pursuit: “Turn back this way, Búcar! You came from over the sea; now you shall meet the Çid, him of the great beard. We two shall greet each other and strike up a friendship.”
sentences.n: ca[d]iól = cadió + le, 'fell (in pursuit) on him', cadió the old preterite of caer (= cayó), the d Pidal's; al rey Búcar names the le in advance. Acá torna, imperative, 'turn back here', closed with ! and no ¡, as printed. venist, 'you came', preterite 2nd singular (= viniste): the Çid speaks to his enemy with tú. dalent mar = d'alent mar, 'from beyond the sea', alent being a form of allén (v. 2425): Búcar has come over from Morocco. Ve[e]rte as, the split future, 'you will see yourself' (= te verás), veerse con uno, 'to meet with someone'; veer = ver, the second e Pidal's; as = has. el de la barba grant, 'he of the great beard', the Çid naming himself by his pride; the print has graut, a turned n, read as grant (the phrase is barba grant elsewhere). saludar nos hemos, the split future again, 'we shall greet each other'. Pidal's note to v. 2411: 'nos besaremos (comp. 3030) y pactaremos amistad' — 'we shall kiss each other and make a pact of friendship'. tajar amiztad, literally 'to cut friendship', as one cuts a bargain; amizta[t], the t Pidal's, z as printed. The greeting and the pact are grim irony: the meeting will be with the sword.

sentences.i: Búcar answered the Çid: “God confound such friendship! You have a sword in your hand and I see you spurring on; by the look of it, you mean to try it out on me.
sentences.n: Respuso = respondió, the old strong preterite (v. 979). cofonda, present subjunctive of cofonder (= confundir), a curse: 'may God confound'; closed with ! and no ¡, as printed. veot = veo + te, 'I see you'; aguijar, 'to spur on'. así commo semeja, 'as it seems'. mi unaccented, as printed. Pidal's note: ensayar, 'probar, emplear', v. 2376 — 'to try, put to use', the first of the three senses of ensayar met in the last part. He adds: La persecución de Búcar, uno de los episodios más famoso del Poema, p. 49, 50, n. y 51 — 'the pursuit of Búcar, one of the most famous episodes of the poem' (pages of his introduction; famoso, for famosos, as printed).

sentences.t:
Mas si el cavallo non estropieça o comigo non ca[d]e,
non te juntarás comigo fata dentro en la mar.”
Aquí respuso mio Çid: “esto non será verdad.”
sentences.l:
But if the horse not stumbles or with-me not falls,
not yourself you-will-join with-me until inside in the sea.”
Here replied my Çid: “this not will-be true.”
sentences.i: But unless my horse stumbles or falls with me, you will not come up with me till we are out in the sea.” To this my Çid replied: “That shall not be so.”
sentences.n: estropieça, 'stumbles' (estropeçar = tropezar). comigo non ca[d]e, 'does not fall with me'; cade = cae, the d Pidal's; the line ends in á-e. non te juntarás comigo, 'you will not join yourself to me', not catch up with me. fata = hasta (f- for h-); dentro en la mar, 'right into the sea', where his ships lie; mar here feminine. Aquí, 'here, at this'. Pidal's note: 'esto no será así'; comp. 979 — 'this will not be so', the same turn as at v. 979.

sentences.t:
Buen cavallo tiene Búcar e grandes saltos faz,
mas Bavieca el de mio Çid alcançándolo va.
sentences.l:
Good horse has Búcar and great leaps makes,
but Bavieca the-one of my Çid overtaking-him goes.
sentences.i: Búcar has a good horse, and it takes great bounds; but Babieca, my Çid's horse, is gaining on him.
sentences.n: faz = faze (haze), 'makes', the cut-down form, with f- for modern h-. Bavieca el de mio Çid, 'Babieca, the (horse) of my Çid'. alcançándolo va, ir + gerund with lo glued on, 'goes overtaking him', closing the gap. The presents tiene, faz, va put the chase before the hearers' eyes.

sentences.t:
Alcançólo el Çid a Búcar a tres braças del mar,
arriba alçó Colada, un grant colpe dádol ha,
las carbonclas del yelmo tollidas gela[s] ha,
sentences.l:
Overtook-him the Çid Búcar at three fathoms from-the sea,
up he-raised Colada, a great blow given-him he-has,
the carbuncles of-the helmet taken-away from-him-[them] he-has,
sentences.i: The Çid overtook Búcar three fathoms from the sea; he raised Colada high and dealt him a great blow; he struck the carbuncles from his helmet,
sentences.n: Alcançólo … a Búcar, the object given twice, lo and a Búcar (as at v. 2408). braças, 'fathoms', the span of the outstretched arms (braço): three fathoms short of the water. Colada, the sword the Çid won at Tévar. dádol ha = dádo + l(e) + ha, 'he has given him', the pronoun glued to the participle; the preterite alçó and the perfect ha dado stand side by side. carbonclas, 'carbuncles', red stones set in the helmet as ornament. tollidas gela[s] ha, 'he has taken them from him': toller, 'to take away', its participle agreeing with las carbonclas; gelas = ge + las, ge 'from him', the s Pidal's. Pidal's note to v. 2422: Comp. 766 — the same stroke Martín Antolínez dealt Galve (echógelas aparte).

sentences.t:
cortól el yelmo e, librado todo lo al,
fata la çintura el espada llegado ha.
sentences.l:
cut-to-him the helmet and, dispatched all the other,
as-far-as the waist the sword arrived has.
sentences.i: cut through his helmet and, cleaving all the rest, the sword went down as far as his waist.
sentences.n: cortól = cortó + le, 'cut his (helmet)', as at v. 767. librado todo lo al, an absolute participle, 'all the rest being dispatched': al, 'other thing, the rest' (neuter, Latin alius). librar is taken here as 'to get through, finish with', the blade going through all that lay beneath the helmet; Pidal gives no note, and the exact shade of librado is not certain. el espada, el before a vowel for la. llegado ha = ha llegado, the participle before its auxiliary, 'has reached'. The stroke that splits a man to the waist is the epic's great blow (compare v. 751).

sentences.t:
Mató a Búcar, al rey de allén mar,
e ganó a Tizón que mill marcos d' oro val.
sentences.l:
He-killed Búcar, the king from beyond sea,
and won Tizón that thousand marks of gold is-worth.
sentences.i: He killed Búcar, the king from beyond the sea, and won Tizón, a sword worth a thousand marks of gold.
sentences.n: Mató a Búcar, al rey, the personal a, repeated in apposition. allén mar, 'beyond the sea' (= allende). ganó a Tizón, the personal a before a named sword, as with Colada (hi gañó a Colada que más vale de mill marcos, v. 1010: Tizón is priced like its fellow). Tizón, 'firebrand', the second of the Çid's two great swords. mill marcos d' oro, 'a thousand marks of gold', the mark a weight of gold or silver; d' printed with a space after the apostrophe. val = vale, cut-down present, 'is worth'.

sentences.t:
Vençió la batalla maravillosa e grant,
Aquís ondró mio Çid e quantos con el[le] [están].
sentences.l:
He-won the battle marvellous and great,
Here-himself honoured my Çid and as-many-as with him [are].
sentences.i: He won the battle, marvellous and great. There my Çid won honour for himself, he and all who are with him.
sentences.n: Vençió, 'he won, conquered'. The comma at the end of the line and the capital that follows are as printed. Aquís = aquí + se, 'here … himself': ondrarse, 'to win honour'. quantos, 'as many as, all who'. el[le] = él, the long form elle with paragogic -e, the le Pidal's (the establishing run is not certain the first l is roman). The whole word [están] is his restoration, closing the tirada on stressed á. Tirada 118 ends here.

sentences.t:
Con estas ganançias yas ivan tornando;
sabet, todos de firme robavan el campo.
sentences.l:
With these gains already-themselves they-were-going returning;
know, all firmly were-plundering the field.
sentences.i: With these spoils they were now turning back; and know this, all of them were stripping the field in earnest.
sentences.n: Tirada 119 (assonance á-o) — the Çid's men come back from the pursuit; the Çid is pleased with his sons-in-law, and they are ashamed; the spoils of the victory (Pidal: Los del Cid vuelven del alcance.—El Cid satisfecho de sus yernos; éstos avergonzados.—Ganancias de la victoria). The line-ends run tornando, campo, nasco, contado, algo: stressed á, then o. ganançias, 'gains, booty'. yas = ya + se, 'already … themselves' (tornarse, 'to turn back'); ivan tornando, ir + gerund. sabet, 'know ye', the singer's aside. de firme, 'firmly, hard'. robar el campo, 'to strip the field' of its spoil.

sentences.t:
A las tiendas eran llegados [con] el que buen[a] nasco,
Mio Çid R[o]y Diaz, el Campeador contado.
sentences.l:
At the tents were arrived [with] him who (in) a-good (hour) was-born,
My Çid R[o]y Diaz, the Campeador renowned.
sentences.i: They had come back to the tents with him who was born in a good hour, my Çid Ruy Díaz, the renowned Campeador.
sentences.n: eran llegados, ser + participle with a verb of motion, 'they had arrived'. [con], the whole word Pidal's restoration. el que buen[a] nasco: the en buen ora formula with en and ora unsaid, 'he who was born in a good (hour)'; the a of buena is Pidal's; nasco, strong preterite of naçer. Pidal's numbers run 2430, then 2433 on Mio Çid R[o]y Diaz with 2431 unlabelled between: the number 2432 is printed nowhere, but no line is missing on the page and there is no footnote, so the gap lies in the numbering and no verse is lost. R[o]y, the o Pidal's; Diaz unaccented as printed. contado, 'renowned', the Campeador's standing epithet.

sentences.t:
con dos espadas que él preçiava algo
por la matança vinía tan privado,
la cara fronzida e almófar soltado,
cofia sobre los pelos fronzida della yaquanto.
sentences.l:
with two swords that he prized somewhat
through the slaughter he-was-coming so swiftly,
the face gathered and mail-hood loosened,
coif over the hairs gathered of-it somewhat.
sentences.i: With two swords that he prized not a little, he came riding swiftly over the field of slaughter, his face framed in the gathered coif, his mail-hood thrown back, the coif over his hair a little rumpled.
sentences.n: The line opens in lower case after the full stop of v. 2433, as printed: the picture of the Çid runs on. dos espadas, Colada and the new-won Tizón. preçiava algo, 'prized somewhat', an understatement; algo, 'something, somewhat'. vinía = venía. privado, 'quickly' (v. 148). la matança, 'the slaughter', the ground of the killing. fronzida, 'gathered, drawn up in folds' (= fruncida): Pidal (note to v. 1744) takes la cara fronzida of the coif gathered about the face, as with cofia … fronzida here. almófar, 'mail hood', soltado, 'loosened', thrown back once the fighting was over, to cool the head (Pidal, v. 1744). Pidal's note to v. 2437: yaquanto, 'algo'. Para la cofia froncida, comp. 1744 — 'somewhat. For the gathered coif, compare v. 1744'. della yaquanto, 'somewhat of it', a little. pelos, 'hair'.

sentences.t: De todas partes sos vassallos van llegando;
sentences.l: From all parts his vassals go arriving;
sentences.i: From every side his vassals were coming in.
sentences.n: Pidal prints this line here, between 2437 and 2438, with the label 2455: he has moved it and kept its number, which places it, by his count, after v. 2454, where it stood in the manuscript. No footnote on these pages explains the move. The number 2437b is ours, given for the order of reading; Pidal's 2455 is printed again on “Grado a Dios…” below. van llegando, ir + gerund, 'are coming up', a present among pasts. sos = sus.

sentences.t:
algo vi[di]e mio Çid de lo que era pagado,
alçó sos ojos, est[a]va adelant catando,
e vi[d]o venir a Dí[a]go e a Fernando;
amos son fijos del co[m]de don Gonçal[v]o.
sentences.l:
something saw my Çid of what he-was pleased,
he-raised his eyes, he-was ahead looking,
and saw come Dí[a]go and Fernando;
both are sons of-the co[u]nt don Gonçal[v]o.
sentences.i: My Çid saw something that pleased him: he raised his eyes and, looking ahead, saw Diego and Fernando coming; both of them are sons of Count Don Gonzalo.
sentences.n: vi[di]e = veía, imperfect of veer, 'was seeing, saw', the di Pidal's (the establishing run is not certain of the italic's extent, e judged roman). de lo que era pagado, 'with which he was pleased': pagado de, 'satisfied with'. est[a]va adelant catando, estar + gerund, 'was looking ahead', the a Pidal's; catar, 'to look'; adelant = adelante. vi[d]o = vio, preterite, the d Pidal's. a Dí[a]go e a Fernando, the personal a; the a of Díago Pidal's; Fernando here with n. co[m]de, the m his; Gonçal[v]o, the v his: their father, whence the patronymic González.

sentences.i: My Çid was glad, and smiled warmly: “Have you come, my sons-in-law? You are both my sons! I know you are well content with the fighting;
sentences.n: Alegrós = alegró + se, 'rejoiced'. fermoso, as an adverb, 'warmly, graciously'; sonrrisando, 'smiling' (sonrrisar = sonreír). Venides = venís, sodes = sois, the old -des endings. The line opens with ¿ and closes with !, as printed: a question and an exclamation run together. mios fijos sodes amos, 'you are both my sons', the fullest welcome. pagado de, 'satisfied with': de lidiar bien sodes pagados, 'you are well content with fighting'. The Çid means it kindly; the hearers, who have heard of Fernando's flight, may hear it otherwise, and v. 2464 shows how the Infantes take such praise.

sentences.t:
a Carrión de vos irán buenos mandados,
cómmo al rey Búcar avemos arrancado.
Commo yo fio por Dios y en todos los sos santos,
desta arrancada nos iremos pagados.”
sentences.l:
to Carrión of you will-go good tidings,
how the king Búcar we-have routed.
As I trust by God and in all the his saints,
from-this rout we-shall-go satisfied.”
sentences.i: Good tidings of you will go to Carrión, of how we have routed King Búcar. As I trust in God and in all his saints, we shall come away well content from this victory.”
sentences.n: mandados, 'tidings, reports'. cómmo, 'how'. al rey Búcar, the personal a. avemos arrancado, 'we have routed' (arrancar, 'to rout'). fio, 'I trust', unaccented as printed; fiar por, 'to trust in', with por where the next phrase has en. y = e, 'and'. los sos santos, article + possessive. arrancada, 'rout, victory' (Pidal's gloss at v. 2398, 'victoria'). nos iremos pagados, 'we shall go away content' (irse).

sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez came up just then, his shield hanging at his neck and all hacked by swords; there was no counting the lance-blows on it;
sentences.n: essora, 'then, at that moment'. es llegado, 'has arrived', ser + participle. Álbar accented, as printed. Pidal's note to v. 2450: El escudo colgado al cuello, p. 105. Como el escudo era de tabla, conservaba las señales de los golpes de espada y de lanza — 'the shield hung from the neck (p. 105 of his introduction). As the shield was made of wood, it kept the marks of the blows of sword and lance.' espad[ad]o, 'sword-struck', from espada; the ad Pidal's (the establishing run is not certain of the italic's extent). recabdo, 'reckoning, account': non avie recabdo, 'there was no reckoning', aver used impersonally, 'there was'. The print has a stray point after the semicolon; it is dropped.

sentences.i: those who had dealt them had not got their way with him. The blood was trickling down past his elbow; he had killed more than twenty Moors.
sentences.n: gelos = ge + los, 'them to him', the blows. dieran, the -ra form as a pluperfect, 'had given'. Pidal's note: 'no habían logrado su intento', 'no habían salido con la suya' — 'they had not achieved their aim', 'had not got their way': gelo … logrado, 'had gained it from him'. Por el cobdo ayuso, 'down by the elbow' (cobdo = codo; ayuso, 'down'). destellando, 'dripping' (Latin destillare; not modern destellar, 'to flash'), a loose gerund with no main verb. de veínte arriba, 'from twenty upward', more than twenty; veínte accented as printed. ha … matado, the object between auxiliary and participle.

sentences.t:
“Grado a Dios e al padre que está en alto,
e a vos, Çid, que en buen ora f[o]stes nado!
sentences.l:
“Thanks to God and to-the father who is on high,
and to you, Çid, who in good hour were born!
sentences.i: “Thanks be to God, the Father on high, and to you, Çid, who were born in a good hour!
sentences.n: Minaya speaks, though the poem does not name him: he has just come up (v. 2449), and the Çid answers him at v. 2462. Grado a Dios, 'thanks to God', the thanksgiving of v. 8 (grado a tí, señor padre, que estás en alto). e al padre: the e joins two names of the one God, not two persons. Pidal's footnote numbered 2456 reads Conjunción e pleonástica, v. 300 — 'pleonastic conjunction e, v. 300' — and v. 300 has the same a Dios e al Padre spirital (his note to v. 2342, Dios … e el Padre, also points there). f[o]stes = fuistes, 'you were', the o Pidal's; nado = nacido: the en buen ora formula in full. Numbering: Pidal prints the label 2455 on this line and also on the moved line De todas partes … (here 2437b). His footnote 2456 fits this line, not the next, whose e is a plain 'and'; with the missing 2459 below, this suggests the line is really his 2456 and the second 2455 a slip of the print. The print's numbers are kept here; the reading is not certain.

sentences.t:
Matastes a Búcar e arrancamos el canpo.
Todos estos bienes de vos son e de vuestros vassallos.
sentences.l:
You-killed Búcar and we-routed the field.
All these goods of you are and of your vassals.
sentences.i: You have killed Búcar, and we have won the field. All this wealth is yours and your vassals'.
sentences.n: Matastes = matasteis, 'you killed', the old -stes ending. arrancar el canpo, 'to rout (the enemy from) the field', win the battle; canpo with n, as printed (campo at v. 2461). bienes, 'goods, riches': the spoils.

sentences.t:
E vuestros yernos aquí son ensayados,
fartos de lidiar con moros en el campo.”
sentences.l:
And your sons-in-law here are proved,
sated of fighting with Moors in the field.”
sentences.i: And your sons-in-law have proved themselves here, and fought their fill with the Moors in the field.”
sentences.n: Pidal numbers this line 2460 straight after 2458: the number 2459 is printed nowhere, with no line missing on the page and no footnote. If the second label 2455 (on “Grado a Dios…”) is a slip for 2456, as his footnote 2456 suggests, the lines there run 2456–2459 and nothing is skipped; we keep the print's numbers. Pidal's note: 'aquí se han distinguido', v. 2388 — 'here they have distinguished themselves': son ensayados, ensayarse in its third sense, 'to exert oneself, do deeds of prowess' (v. 2388). fartos, 'sated, having had their fill' (= hartos, f- for h-). Minaya's praise is courteous: in the verse that survives the Infantes do nothing of note in the battle, and Fernando's flight is known only from the chronicle prose Pidal sets in the lost folio.

sentences.t:
Dixo mio Çid: “yo desto so pagado;
quando agora son buenos, adelant serán preçiados.”
sentences.l:
Said my Çid: “I of-this am pleased;
when now they-are good, ahead they-will-be prized.”
sentences.i: My Çid said: “I am glad of this; if they are good men now, hereafter they will be held in esteem.”
sentences.n: so = soy. desto = de esto; pagado de, 'pleased with', again. quando, 'when', here near 'since, if': seeing that they are good now. adelant, 'hereafter'. preçiados, 'prized, esteemed'.

sentences.t: Por bien lo dixo el Çid, mas ellos lo touieron a [escarnio].
sentences.l: For good it said the Çid, but they it held as [mockery].
sentences.i: The Çid meant it well, but they took it as mockery.
sentences.n: Por bien, 'in good part, meaning well'. touieron = tovieron (tuvieron), with u for v, as printed; tener a, 'to take as, hold for'. [escarnio], 'mockery, scorn', the whole word Pidal's restoration; it keeps the á-o assonance. The Infantes, knowing what they did in the battle, hear praise as mockery: the rubric's éstos avergonzados, 'they ashamed'.

sentences.i: All the spoils have come to Valencia; my Çid is glad, and all his vassals with him, for each share came to six hundred marks of silver.
sentences.n: Much here is Pidal's: the os of l[os], the dos of gana[dos] and the os of llegad[os] (the establishing run is not certain the d of ganados is italic), and the whole words [sos vassallos] in the next line. Pidal's note: ganados, 'ganancias', v. 481 — 'gains, spoils', the noun. son llegados, 'have arrived'. que, 'for'. Pidal's note to v. 2467: El botín se dividía en raciones, que después se repartían proporcionalmente entre los combatientes — 'the booty was divided into shares, which were then distributed proportionally among the fighters'. raçión, 'share, portion'. ca[di]e = caía, imperfect of caer, 'fell (to)', the di Pidal's (the italic's extent not certain). seys çientos = seiscientos.

sentences.t:
Los yernos de mio Çid quando este aver tomaron
desta arrancada, que lo tenien en so salvo,
cuydaron que en [sos] días nunqua serien minguados.
sentences.i: When the Çid's sons-in-law took this wealth from the victory and had it safe in their keeping, they thought they would never be in want for the rest of their days.
sentences.n: aver, 'wealth, goods', the noun. desta arrancada, 'from this victory'. Pidal's note to v. 2469: en so salvo, 'en su poder', v. 119; 'en seguridad' — 'in their power'; 'in safety'. tenien, imperfect (= tenían). cuydaron = cuidaron, 'they thought' (cuidar, 'to think'). [sos], the whole word Pidal's. nunqua = nunca. serien minguados, 'would be lacking, in want' (= menguados).

sentences.t:
F[o]ron en Valençia muy bien arreados,
conduchos a sazones, buenas pieles e buenos mantos.
Muchos son alegres mio Çid e s[o]s vassallos.
sentences.l:
W[e]re in Valençia very well furnished,
provisions in seasons, good furs and good mantles.
Much are glad my Çid and h[i]s vassals.
sentences.i: In Valencia they were very well provided for: food in its season, fine furs and fine mantles. Right glad are my Çid and his vassals.
sentences.n: F[o]ron = fueron, 'they were', the o Pidal's; the subject is most naturally the Infantes, though it may be the whole company. arreados, 'furnished, provided'. conduchos, 'provisions, victuals'; a sazones, 'in season(s)', food in its due time or in good supply; the exact sense is uncertain. pieles, 'furs'; mantos, 'mantles'. Muchos son alegres, the adverb mucho agreeing in number with the plural subject: 'very glad are'. s[o]s, the o Pidal's. Tirada 119 ends here; the next, which Pidal marks as a repetition (Repetición), turns again to the Çid's joy in his victory and his sons-in-law.
